This has always been a conundrum for me since one of my biggest issues with religion is the indoctrination phase. If I blasted my kids for believing in God, then really my behavior is no different from someone who is pressuring them to believe. Here's what I've discovered with my own kids: nurture the questioning. Yes, it is okay to tell them what you believe. Yes, it's okay for them to hear your opinions about it, so long as they are constructive. I would avoid bashing religion. Make sure they know they can ask questions in favor or against belief without retribution. They will eventually make up their own minds. My youngest daughter actually believes in a God. It makes her little brain feel better knowing that there is a benevolent being in the sky that watches over her. I'm not going to take that away from her. There is nothing wrong with believing in what you want, even if it contradicts the belief system of someone else. What's probably more important for her to know is that a belief system is held in balance with a healthy dose of acceptance for the beliefs of others. That's what I tell my kids anyway.

What opened my eyes at the age of 13 and allowed me to be completely free was a little book called "The Satanic Bible" by Anton Szandor LaVey. I was attracted to LaVey's "Satanism" because it is just atheism in disguise. It's fun, it has an exotic flair to it, and it has at it's core a very down-to-earth, logical, pragmatic approach to life. Later in life I got older, got a job, and became an adult, dabbled in the eastern meditation traditions like buddhism and falun gong. But it was The Satanic Bible that actually set my mind free and opened my eyes. There is nothing "Satanic" about LaVey's Church of Satan, just good ol' fashioned, wholesome atheism with a healthy dose of life-affirming aphorisms.

I have loved ones that believe. I'm always laughing and asking them why they think a certain thing is true. I feel a duty to be openly skeptical with the people I care about. I mean, I care about them.

For a mature 11, maybe she's ready for some George Carlin, with a promise not to go yelling his bits around school. Some Penn Jillette? Maybe she'd like some of the Atheist Experience videos?
Just make her read the bible. It worked for me ;)

Don't indoctrinate her.

Ask her to ask questions. For me, what pushed me into atheism was the circular reasoning behind the existence of God. As a believer at about 10 I would ask "How do I know God exists?" answering "Because it's written in the Bible". But how do we know that the Bible is the word of God? All the arguments were so circular and self referential I could see as a child it didn't make sense.

But crucially noone indoctrinated me into any set of ideas. Don't tell your child to be an atheist or any other religious or political position. Do instruct them to think for themselves.
